prompt: Why does the course keep the Go Playground for small fragments and not for the lessons themselves?
hint: Think about what surrounds the program in every lesson from lesson 4 on.

choices.text: It runs an outdated release of Go
choices.why: The section says nothing about its release. The reason it gives is what the page lacks around the program.

choices.text: There is no terminal, so no `go build`, `go install` or `go doc`
choices.why: Right. It compiles and runs one program; everything the course types around the program has nowhere to go.

choices.text: It cannot compile a program that imports a package
choices.why: Even `hello.go` imports `fmt`, and a program like that is exactly what the Playground runs.

choices.text: It costs your computer too much memory
choices.why: It is the one path that costs your computer nothing: the program runs on a server.

prompt: Go 1.27.1 is unpacked in `/usr/local/go` and you have the archive of a newer release. What do you do first?
hint: What happens to the files the old release has and the new one does not?

choices.text: Unpack the new archive over `/usr/local/go`, so that your settings survive
choices.why: That leaves files of both releases in one tree. Your settings are not in there anyway: they live in your home directory.

choices.text: Delete `/usr/local/go`, then unpack
choices.why: Right. An upgrade is a delete and an unpack, never a merge.

choices.text: Run `go clean -cache`, then unpack the archive
choices.why: The build cache is in `~/.cache/go-build`, not in the toolchain; emptying it leaves `/usr/local/go` as it was.

choices.text: Edit `/usr/local/go/VERSION` to the new number
choices.why: `VERSION` records which release the directory is; changing it changes no program in `bin`.

prompt: The lab downloaded Go 1.27.1 as 75,704,807 bytes, and `du -sh /usr/local/go` then reported `253M`. Roughly how many times more room does the toolchain take on disk than the download? Give a whole number.
hint: About 76 MB against 253 MB.

prompt: A student on Windows wants every transcript in the course to match what they see, including `file` and `du`. Which path fits?
hint: Go itself behaves the same everywhere; the commands around it do not.

choices.text: The installer from go.dev/dl, because `go version` prints the same on every system
choices.why: Go would work, but the shell around it is Windows's, and the section names `file` and `du` as missing there.

choices.text: The Playground, since its server runs Linux
choices.why: Whatever its server runs, the page has no terminal, so there is no `du` to type.

choices.text: A Linux virtual machine, such as WSL, with Go installed inside it
choices.why: Right. Inside an Ubuntu machine the transcripts match byte for byte, prompt and all; the price is disk and memory.

choices.text: Any path at all, because transcripts only show Go's own output
choices.why: They also show `ls`, `du`, `file` and the shell's own messages, like exit status 127.

prompt: Unpacking the archive does not make `go` a command: the shell runs only programs that sit in a directory listed in the variable `___`.
hint: Ana changed it in `~/.profile`.

prompt: Ana's second line in `~/.profile` adds `$HOME/go/bin`. Which programs is it for?
hint: Lesson 4 runs `hello` by name from `~`.

choices.text: `go` and `gofmt`
choices.why: Those are in `/usr/local/go/bin`, which the first line adds.

choices.text: The ones you build with `go install`
choices.why: Right. `go install` puts them in `~/go/bin`, `GOBIN`, and this line lets the shell find them.

choices.text: The modules that `go get` downloads into the module cache
choices.why: Downloaded modules go to `~/go/pkg/mod` as source, and nothing there is run by name.

choices.text: The compiled packages that make a second `go run` fast
choices.why: Those are in the build cache, `~/.cache/go-build`, which is not in `PATH` and need not be.

prompt: Match each setting `go env` printed with what it holds.
hint: Three directories, and two of the values are inside one of them.

pairs.right: the toolchain and the standard library's source

prompt: A machine's shell exports `GOPROXY=off`, and Ana's `go env -w` file says `GOPROXY=https://proxy.golang.org,direct`. Downloads fail with `module lookup disabled by GOPROXY=off`. Does `go env -u GOPROXY` fix it?
hint: Which of the three places wins, and which one does `-u` edit?

choices.text: Yes, because the last command typed wins
choices.why: The order is fixed by where a value comes from, not by when it was typed: `go env -w GOTOOLCHAIN=auto` was typed last and lost.

choices.text: Yes, since `-u` restores the release's `go.env` default
choices.why: It removes the line from Ana's file, but the environment sits above both files and still says `off`.

choices.text: No: `-u` edits only her own file, and the environment still wins
choices.why: Right. The shell's `GOPROXY=off` beats both files; it has to be removed from the environment itself.

choices.text: No: `GOPROXY` cannot be changed after installation
choices.why: Every setting can be changed, in any of the three places; the question is which place wins.

prompt: Which file did `go env -w GOTOOLCHAIN=auto` write to?
hint: Ana printed it with `cat` right afterwards.

choices.text: `/usr/local/go/go.env`
choices.why: That file ships with the release, inside `GOROOT`, and you never write in it.

choices.text: `~/.config/go/env`
choices.why: Right. `go env -w` keeps your own settings there, the middle one of the three places.

choices.text: `~/.profile`, beside the two `PATH` lines
choices.why: `~/.profile` belongs to the shell, and Ana edited it herself with `echo`.

choices.text: The `go.mod` of the current module
choices.why: `go env -w` changes settings for every module you build, not for one.

prompt: With `GO111MODULE=off`, where did the go command search for an imported package?
hint: The error listed every place it searched.

choices.text: Wherever a `go.mod` named it
choices.why: That is module mode, the one in use today. GOPATH mode never read a `go.mod`.

choices.text: Under `src` in two roots, `$GOROOT` and `$GOPATH`, in a directory named after the import path
choices.why: Right. An import path was a directory under one of two roots, and those two lines were the whole search.

choices.text: In the directories listed by `go.work`
choices.why: Workspaces belong to module mode; the GOPATH-mode error never mentioned one.

choices.text: At the module proxy, `proxy.golang.org`
choices.why: GOPATH mode searched only the disk, and the message names two directories, not a server.

prompt: Which of these does `~/go` hold today? Choose all that apply.
hint: `ls ~/go ~/go/pkg` printed it.

choices.text: `bin`, where `go install` puts programs
choices.why: Yes. It is `GOBIN` unless you set it elsewhere.

choices.text: `src`, where your projects have to live
choices.why: That was GOPATH mode. There was no `src` in Ana's `~/go`, and her code lives in `~/hello` and `~/setup-work`.

choices.text: `pkg/mod`, the downloaded modules
choices.why: Yes, the module cache, `GOMODCACHE`.

choices.text: the standard library's source
choices.why: That is in `/usr/local/go/src`, part of the toolchain, `GOROOT`.

prompt: Inside `~/setup-work/hello`, `go run .` suggested `go get example.com/greet`. Why is that the wrong fix here?
hint: Where does `go get` look, and where is `greet`?

choices.text: `go get` works only for packages of the standard library
choices.why: It is the opposite: the standard library is already there, and `go get` fetches everything else.

choices.text: It would look on the network, and `greet` is only on this disk
choices.why: Right. A workspace is how you say "use my copy", without publishing anything.

choices.text: Because `greet` has no `go.mod` of its own
choices.why: It has one: `find` listed `./greet/go.mod`.

choices.text: `go get` writes `go.work`, and the workspace has to be made by hand
choices.why: `go get` edits `go.mod`; `go work init` and `go work use` are what wrote `go.work`.

prompt: A teammate copies only the `hello` directory from `~/setup-work` to their own machine and types `go run .` in it. What happens?
hint: Look at what `hello/go.mod` said after the workspace existed.

choices.text: It prints `Hello, Ana`, since `go work use` recorded `greet` in `hello/go.mod`
choices.why: `hello/go.mod` did not change: it still named no dependency after the workspace was made.

choices.text: It fails: nothing in `hello` says where `example.com/greet` is
choices.why: Right. The workspace lives beside the modules, so it stayed behind with `greet`.

choices.text: It prints `Hello, Ana`; the go command fetches `greet` from Ana's workspace
choices.why: A workspace is a file on Ana's disk, not a server anybody can reach.

choices.text: It fails, because `go.work` says `go 1.27.1`
choices.why: The teammate has no `go.work` at all, so its `go` line plays no part.

prompt: `go version` answers `bash: line 1: go: command not found` and exit status 127. What does that tell you?
hint: Which program printed the message?

choices.text: The Go installation is damaged and has to be unpacked again
choices.why: Go never ran. The same installation worked as soon as `~/.profile` was read again.

choices.text: The shell found no `go` in any directory of `PATH`
choices.why: Right. 127 is `bash`'s number for no such command; only `PATH` is wrong.

choices.text: The module needs a newer Go than the one installed
choices.why: That refusal comes from the go command itself, and it names both versions.

choices.text: `go version` needs a `go.mod` in the current directory
choices.why: `go version` ran in `~/setup`, which has no `go.mod`, and printed the release.

prompt: `go: go.mod requires go >= 1.28 (running go 1.27.1; GOTOOLCHAIN=local)`. Which response hides the message without solving anything?
hint: Which one changes what the module says, rather than which Go runs it?

choices.text: Installing the newer release the way section 02 did
choices.why: That solves it: the module gets the Go it was written for.

choices.text: Letting the go command fetch the release by not forcing `local`
choices.why: That solves it too, when the release exists: with `auto` the go command downloads it.

choices.text: Lowering the `go` line in `go.mod`
choices.why: Right. The code still uses whatever it was written with, and if 1.27.1 lacks it the failure returns as a harder compile error.

choices.text: Running it on a machine that already has a newer Go installed
choices.why: That works; the message only says this toolchain is older than the module wants.

prompt: Put the parts of the failed download's message in the order it prints them.
hint: It reads from what was wanted to why it was not had.

prompt: You unpacked Go 1.27.1 into `/usr/local/go`, but `go version` prints an older release. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Which `go` does the shell run when there are two?

choices.text: The build cache still holds the older compiler
choices.why: The cache holds compiled packages, not the `go` program; which `go` runs is decided before the cache is ever read.

choices.text: `GOTOOLCHAIN=local` forces the oldest release on the machine
choices.why: `local` means the toolchain that is running, whichever it is, and no download; it picks nothing older.

choices.text: The new archive was unpacked over the old tree
choices.why: That mixes files and breaks builds, but `bin/go` would still be the new program and print the new release.

choices.text: Another `go` comes earlier in `PATH`, which `command -v go` reveals
choices.why: Right. The shell runs the first `go` it finds, perhaps one a package manager put there years ago.

prompt: Which of these can you delete and get back by building or downloading again? Choose all that apply.
hint: Separate what the go command owns from what you wrote.

choices.text: `~/.cache/go-build`
choices.why: Yes. `go clean -cache` empties it, and the next build fills it again, more slowly once.

choices.text: `~/go/pkg/mod`
choices.why: Yes. The modules come back from the proxy the next time a build needs them.

choices.text: `~/setup-work/go.work`
choices.why: You wrote that with `go work init` and `go work use`; nothing makes it again by itself.

choices.text: `/usr/local/go/src`
choices.why: That is the standard library's source inside the toolchain; only unpacking a release again brings it back.

prompt: `go work init ./hello` created the workspace, and `go work ___ ./greet` added the second module to it.
hint: The directive inside `go.work` has the same name.

prompt: On a new laptop, `go install` succeeds in a module, but typing the program's name answers `command not found`. Which line is missing from `~/.profile`?
hint: `go install` itself ran, so one of the two lines must be there.

choices.text: `export PATH=$PATH:/usr/local/go/bin`
choices.why: Without that one, `go install` itself would have been `command not found`.

choices.text: `export PATH=$PATH:$HOME/go/bin`
choices.why: Right. The program was installed in `~/go/bin`, and the shell only looks there if `PATH` says so.

choices.text: A `go env -w GOBIN=~/go/bin` line, so that `go install` knows where to put programs
choices.why: `go install` already put it in `~/go/bin` by default; the shell is what cannot find it.

choices.text: A line creating `go.work` in the home directory
choices.why: A workspace decides which modules build together, never which programs the shell can run.
